library(sommer)

A field guide to GLMMs in sommer

This vignette develops the statistical model behind the generalized linear mixed-model (GLMM) methods in sommer, explains the two fitting routes, describes their parameterizations, and connects them to covariance structures, prediction, uncertainty, and diagnostics. It is intended as a theoretical companion to the shorter GLMM user guide. The guide is not a claim that every estimator has the same inferential properties or that every family and covariance structure can be combined on every route.

The central modeling idea is simple: specify a probability model for each observation conditional on latent random effects, and give those random effects the structured covariance model familiar from linear mixed models. The numerical challenge is that integrating over the latent effects is generally not analytic. sommer therefore offers a penalized quasi-likelihood (PQL) route and an opt-in native Laplace-likelihood route. They target related models, but they are different approximations and should not be treated as interchangeable likelihood analyses.

1. The model

1.1 Conditional response distributions

Let \(y_i\) denote observation \(i\), and let \(u\) collect all random effects. Conditional on \(u\), the observations are modeled as independent, with conditional means \(\mu_i\) and a specified exponential-family or other supported response distribution:

\[ y_i \mid u \sim f_i(y_i \mid \mu_i, \phi_i), \qquad g_i(\mu_i) = \eta_i = o_i + x_i^\mathsf{T}\beta + z_i^\mathsf{T}u. \]

Here \(g_i\) is the link, \(o_i\) is an optional offset, \(x_i\) and \(z_i\) are design rows, and \(\beta\) contains fixed effects. The conditional mean and variance are functions of the family parameters:

\[ \operatorname{E}(y_i\mid u)=\mu_i,\qquad \operatorname{Var}(y_i\mid u)=\phi_i V_i(\mu_i). \]

For Bernoulli and Poisson families, dispersion is fixed by the distribution. For other families, dispersion or shape parameters may be estimated or fixed where the selected family and fitting method support them.

The random effects follow a zero-mean multivariate normal distribution,

\[ u \sim N(0,G(\theta)), \]

where \(\theta\) denotes covariance parameters. In sommer, the covariance matrix is assembled from the random-effect terms, their covariance descriptors, and any supplied relationship matrices. Thus the fixed-effect formula describes the conditional linear predictor, while random and its covariance structures describe the latent Gaussian distribution.

1.2 Conditional and marginal quantities

The model is specified conditionally on \(u\). Its inverse-link mean \(g^{-1}(x_i^\mathsf{T}\beta+z_i^\mathsf{T}u+o_i)\) is generally not the mean after integrating over the random effects:

\[ \operatorname{E}(y_i\mid x_i) = \operatorname{E}_{u}\!\left[ g^{-1}(o_i+x_i^\mathsf{T}\beta+z_i^\mathsf{T}u) \right]. \]

For a nonlinear inverse link, this integral usually differs from \(g^{-1}(o_i+x_i^\mathsf{T}\beta)\), the response mean at zero random effects. For example, with a log link and a Gaussian random intercept \(u\sim N(0,\sigma_u^2)\),

\[ \operatorname{E}_{u}\{\exp(\eta+u)\} =\exp(\eta+\sigma_u^2/2), \]

whereas setting \(u=0\) gives \(\exp(\eta)\). This distinction is essential when describing predictions: a conditional prediction, a zero-random-effect prediction, and a population-integrated prediction answer different questions.

1.3 A concrete binary example

For a Bernoulli-logit model with subject intercepts,

\[ y_{ij}\mid u_j\sim \operatorname{Bernoulli}(p_{ij}),\qquad \operatorname{logit}(p_{ij}) =\beta_0+\beta_1 x_{ij}+u_j,\qquad u_j\sim N(0,\sigma_u^2). \]

The coefficient \(\beta_1\) is a conditional log-odds contrast, holding the latent subject effect fixed. It is not, in general, the log odds ratio obtained after averaging predicted probabilities over subjects. The random intercept induces within-subject dependence even though observations are independent conditional on that intercept.

2. Covariance structures and random effects

2.1 Covariance of coefficient blocks

A random term can have one or more coefficients per level. For example, a random intercept-and-slope model has a two-dimensional covariance matrix \(\Sigma\) for the intercept and slope. If the levels also have a known relationship matrix \(A\), the coefficient covariance has a Kronecker-product structure, with ordering determined by the model design:

\[ \operatorname{Var}(u) \ \text{has the structure}\ \Sigma\otimes A. \]

Equivalently, its precision is assembled from the inverse descriptor and the relationship precision. An identity relationship gives independent levels; a pedigree or genomic relationship matrix couples their effects. The covariance descriptor controls covariance among coefficient dimensions, while the relationship matrix controls covariance among levels.

This separation is one of sommer’s key modeling capabilities. Structures such as unstructured, diagonal, compound-symmetric, autoregressive, factor analytic, and reduced-rank forms constrain \(\Sigma\) in different ways. Random slopes, multi-trait effects, genotype-by-environment terms, and relationship-informed genetic effects can therefore be expressed using the same underlying idea as in Gaussian mixed models. The existence of a covariance structure in the package does not imply that every structure is eligible in every GLMM engine; consult the GLMM guide and inspect the execution plan for the selected route.

2.2 Conditional independence is not marginal independence

For the likelihood methods described below, observation densities factor conditional on \(u\):

\[ p(y\mid u,\beta,\theta)=\prod_i p(y_i\mid u,\beta). \]

After integrating over \(u\), this product no longer factors across observations that share random effects. A random intercept therefore captures dependence through the shared latent variable; it is not an extra residual correlation term added independently to each response distribution.

PQL’s working Gaussian problem can use rcov and other supported working covariance structures. Native Laplace instead uses the conditional observation likelihood and the random-effect covariance. It currently does not accept structured residual covariance or the supplied observation precision matrix W.

2.3 Formulae and covariance specification

The syntax for fixed and random effects follows the usual mmes() conventions. For example:

fit <- mmes(
  count ~ treatment + offset(log(exposure)),
  random = ~ site,
  data = dat,
  family = poisson(),
  control = mmes_control(
    task = list(objective = "ml",
      glmm = list(method = "laplace"))
  )
)

The offset is known and enters the linear predictor with coefficient fixed at one. In a log-rate model, offset(log(exposure)) makes the expected count proportional to exposure while the fixed and random effects describe the log-rate.

3. Response families and parameterizations

The table gives the main conditional mean/variance parameterizations relevant to the native Laplace route. The PQL route delegates family operations to family objects and has a different support envelope.

Family Conditional mean Conditional variance Native Laplace link(s)
Binomial \(p\) \(p(1-p)/m\) for \(m\) trials logit, probit, complementary log-log
Poisson \(\lambda\) \(\lambda\) log
Negative binomial NB2 \(\mu\) \(\mu+\mu^2/\theta\) log
Gaussian \(\mu\) \(\phi\) identity
Gamma \(\mu\) \(\phi\mu^2\) log
Zero-inflated Poisson \((1-\pi)\lambda\) \((1-\pi)\lambda+(1-\pi)\pi\lambda^2\) log for \(\lambda\)

For grouped binomial data, \(m\) is the number of trials. binm(successes, trials=...) represents a proportion with its trial count attached, and the native Laplace method also accepts a two-column successes/failures response. With a mixed-family model, trial counts can be provided through the documented familym() interface. Supplying proportions without their denominator loses information about their precision.

3.1 Negative binomial and dispersion parameters

The NB2 parameter \(\theta\) is a positive shape parameter. Large \(\theta\) approaches the Poisson variance; smaller \(\theta\) allows greater overdispersion. On the native Laplace route, it may be estimated jointly or fixed with task$glmm$familyParameters. Gaussian dispersion is residual variance \(\phi\). Gamma dispersion satisfies \(\operatorname{Var}(Y\mid u)=\phi\mu^2\), so the Gamma shape is \(1/\phi\). Family-specific parameter estimates are reported on their natural scale.

Dispersion should not be used as a substitute for omitted structure. Overdispersion may arise from latent heterogeneity, excess zeros, dependence, or an incorrect mean model, and those mechanisms imply different interpretations and predictions.

3.2 Zero-inflated Poisson

The current M5 implementation is a restricted zero-inflated Poisson (ZIP) model. Let \(S_i\) indicate membership in a structural-zero state:

\[ S_i\sim\operatorname{Bernoulli}(\pi),\qquad Y_i = \begin{cases} 0, & S_i=1,\\ \operatorname{Poisson}(\lambda_i), & S_i=0, \end{cases} \qquad \log(\lambda_i)=\eta_i. \]

Consequently,

\[ \Pr(Y_i=0)=\pi+(1-\pi)e^{-\lambda_i},\quad \Pr(Y_i=y>0)=(1-\pi)e^{-\lambda_i}\frac{\lambda_i^y}{y!}, \]

and

\[ \operatorname{E}(Y_i\mid u)=(1-\pi)\lambda_i,\qquad \operatorname{Var}(Y_i\mid u) =(1-\pi)\lambda_i+(1-\pi)\pi\lambda_i^2. \]

zipoisson() estimates one common intercept-only structural-zero probability by default. The count component’s linear predictor models \(\log(\lambda_i)\); the fitted response mean is \((1-\pi)\lambda_i\). The probability can be fixed or estimated using task$glmm$familyParameters. A separate fixed-effects formula, zipoisson(zero=~covariates), extends this to \(\operatorname{logit}(\pi_i)=a_i+w_i^\mathsf{T}\gamma\), with its own offset \(a_i\) and fixed design \(w_i\). Its logit coefficients are jointly optimized with the count coefficients and covariance parameters and appear in zeroCoefficients; summary() computes their SEs only after fitting. The mixture mean and variance above then use \(\pi_i\) row by row. The default zero=~1 preserves the scalar family-parameter interface. Zero-component random effects remain unsupported. ZIP is not a hurdle model: zeros may arise from either component, and positive counts follow a zero-truncated Poisson distribution conditional on positivity.

For a zero formula, \(\exp(\gamma_j)\) is a structural-zero odds ratio conditional on the other zero covariates, not a count rate ratio. A covariate present in both components can change the observed mean through both predictors:

\[ \frac{\partial\log\{\operatorname{E}(Y_i\mid u)\}}{\partial x} =\beta_x-\pi_i\gamma_x \]

when \(x\) enters both linear predictors without transformations or interactions. Count and zero coefficients must therefore not be interpreted as two independent regressions on observed positives and zeros.

To see why, let \(\tau_i=\Pr(S_i=1\mid Y_i,u)\) under the fitted model. For a positive observation \(\tau_i=0\); for a zero,

\[ \tau_i=\frac{\pi_i}{\pi_i+(1-\pi_i)\exp(-\lambda_i)},\qquad \frac{\partial\log p(Y_i\mid u)}{\partial\gamma} =w_i(\tau_i-\pi_i). \]

An observed zero does not reveal which component generated it. The native optimizer differentiates the complete marginal Laplace approximation, including the mode and determinant corrections, rather than merely summing these conditional scores. Zero coefficients enter the same joint outer parameter vector as count coefficients and covariance parameters. There is no second latent random-effect block for the zero predictor.

The null case \(\pi=0\) is a boundary of the parameter space. Standard interior-point Wald approximations are not automatically valid there, and near-zero inflation can be weakly identified from the Poisson count mean. Model convergence alone does not establish that the ZIP component is identified. Use simulation-based calibration, boundary diagnostics, and scientific justification before interpreting \(\pi\).

3.3 Mixed families and long data

familym() assigns a response family to each trait label in a long-format data set. Conditional on the shared random effects, each row contributes its own family density. Random-effect structures may link traits, but the likelihood still uses each row’s declared observation family and its appropriate trials or family parameters.

fit <- mmes(
  value ~ trait - 1 + trait:environment,
  random = ~ vsm(usm(trait), ism(genotype)),
  data = long_data,
  family = familym(
    "trait",
    disease = binomial("probit"),
    count = nbinom2(theta = 2),
    biomass = Gamma("log"),
    yield = gaussian()
  ),
  control = mmes_control(
    task = list(objective = "ml",
      glmm = list(method = "laplace",
        familyParameters = list(
          count = list(theta = 2, estimate = TRUE),
          biomass = list(dispersion = 0.4, estimate = TRUE),
          yield = list(dispersion = 1, estimate = FALSE)
        )))
  )
)

The family-specific likelihood is useful for heterogeneous traits, but it does not make the residual covariance structure of a Gaussian multivariate model available to the native Laplace likelihood. Model the cross-trait dependence through eligible shared random effects.

4. Fitting route one: PQL and IRLS

4.1 The working response

PQL replaces the nonlinear response model, locally at the current predictor, with a weighted Gaussian working problem. At outer iteration \(t\), define

\[ \mu_i^{(t)}=g^{-1}(\eta_i^{(t)}),\qquad h_i^{(t)}=\frac{d\mu_i}{d\eta_i}\bigg|_{\eta_i^{(t)}},\qquad V_i^{(t)}=V_i(\mu_i^{(t)}). \]

With prior precision weight \(w_i\) (for example, binomial trial count), the working response and working precision are

\[ z_i^{(t)} =\eta_i^{(t)}+\frac{y_i-\mu_i^{(t)}}{h_i^{(t)}}-o_i, \qquad d_i^{(t)}=w_i\frac{(h_i^{(t)})^2}{V_i^{(t)}}. \]

The offset is removed from \(z_i\) because it remains fixed and known in the linear predictor. sommer passes this working response and precision to its existing weighted Gaussian mixed-model machinery. That inner fit updates fixed effects, random-effect predictions, and covariance parameters. The linear predictor is refreshed and the process repeats until the PQL convergence criterion is met.

This procedure is computationally attractive because it reuses established Gaussian solvers and their covariance machinery. But iteratively solving working Gaussian models is not the same as maximizing the integrated GLMM likelihood. PQL estimates and standard errors can be biased for binary, rare-event, or sparse-count data, especially with substantial random-effect variance. Convergence of the outer iteration is numerical convergence of the chosen approximation, not proof of unbiasedness.

4.2 PQL usage and controls

PQL remains the default non-Gaussian route. task$pql$maxit, task$pql$tol, and the warm-start option govern the outer procedure. Other mmes_control() settings configure the Gaussian inner fit and therefore depend on the selected Gaussian engine and covariance model.

fit_pql <- mmes(
  response ~ treatment,
  random = ~ subject,
  rcov = ~ units,
  data = dat,
  family = binomial(),
  control = mmes_control(
    task = list(pql = list(maxit = 30L, tol = 1e-5))
  )
)

The actual supported families, response representation, rcov, weights, and random structures depend on the PQL path. In particular, the native ZIP family is Laplace-only. Consult the current GLMM guide rather than assuming that a family supported by stats::glm() can be combined with every mmes() mixed-model option.

5. Fitting route two: native Laplace likelihood

5.1 Integrating out random effects

The marginal likelihood is

\[ L(\beta,\theta,\psi;y) =\int \left\{\prod_i p(y_i\mid u,\beta,\psi)\right\} \varphi(u;0,G(\theta))\,du, \]

where \(\psi\) collects any estimated family parameters. Except for special cases, this integral has no closed form. Define the log joint density \(h(u)\) as the conditional observation log likelihood plus the Gaussian random-effect log density. Its conditional mode is

\[ \widehat u=\operatorname*{arg\,max}_u h(u), \qquad H=-\frac{\partial^2h(u)}{\partial u\,\partial u^\mathsf{T}} \bigg|_{u=\widehat u}. \]

The Laplace approximation to the marginal log likelihood is

\[ \ell_{\mathrm{LA}}(\beta,\theta,\psi) \approx h(\widehat u) +\frac{q}{2}\log(2\pi)-\frac{1}{2}\log|H|, \]

with \(q=\dim(u)\). This is a local Gaussian approximation to the integral around its mode. It is exact when the log joint density is quadratic in \(u\), as in a Gaussian response with a Gaussian random effect. For non-Gaussian families, accuracy depends on how well the local curvature represents the integral; small numbers of independent clusters, sparse data, and strongly skewed conditional posteriors warrant special care.

5.2 Numerical optimization in sommer

The native route obtains fixed/random designs and covariance descriptors through sommer’s model-preparation machinery. It then uses a sparse Newton-type solve to find the conditional random-effect mode and evaluate its Hessian determinant. The outer nlminb optimization jointly updates fixed effects, free covariance parameters, and any free family parameters using native first scores of the marginal Laplace objective. It is an ML method, not REML.

This architecture preserves the meaning of the random-effect covariance structures and avoids treating a Gaussian AI-REML score as if it were the gradient of a non-Gaussian likelihood. The Gaussian objective and AI-REML engines remain distinct. The optimizer’s first derivatives include dependence of both the mode and the determinant correction on the parameters. Numerical second derivatives are calculated on demand for uncertainty, after fitting.

fit_laplace <- mmes(
  outcome ~ treatment,
  random = ~ subject,
  data = dat,
  family = binomial(),
  control = mmes_control(
    task = list(objective = "ml",
      glmm = list(method = "laplace",
        maxit = 1000L, modeMaxit = 100L, modeTol = 1e-8))
  )
)
logLik(fit_laplace)
AIC(fit_laplace)
fit_laplace$laplaceDiagnostics

maxit controls the outer optimizer. modeMaxit and modeTol control the inner conditional-mode solve. These are GLMM-specific controls; Gaussian AI-REML iteration and proposal settings do not control the Laplace optimizer. Inspect the optimizer result, convergence, gradient, laplaceDiagnostics, and executionPlan, rather than treating a returned object as sufficient evidence of a well-behaved fit.

5.3 Supported set and deliberate restrictions

Native Laplace currently supports the documented binomial, Poisson, ZIP, NB2, Gaussian, and Gamma family/link combinations, including long-format familym() models. It reuses sommer covariance and relationship precision descriptors where supported by the native setup. It requires ML, Henderson formulation, a full-rank fixed-effects design, at least one random term, and output$inverse=0 during fitting.

Structured residual covariance, W, weights formulas, vcc, direct formulation, known-covariance solve mode, arbitrary user-defined likelihoods, hurdle models, zero-inflated NB2, and random effects in the ZIP zero component are not supported on this route. Unsupported settings are rejected rather than silently interpreted as Gaussian-engine controls. These limits matter when comparing models: a familiar covariance syntax doesn’t establish that it is accepted or scientifically identical for the selected likelihood.

6. Estimation, uncertainty, and PEV

6.1 Point estimates are not uncertainty estimates

An optimizer can converge while the likelihood is nearly flat, parameters are at a boundary, or the Hessian is indefinite. In the native Laplace method, summary() and vcov() request a numerical Hessian of the joint outer objective after fitting. Local standard errors are reported only when the fit converged, is not flagged near a boundary, and the joint curvature is positive-definite and numerically nonsingular. Covariance and family parameter standard errors are transformed to the natural scale using the delta method.

These are local curvature approximations, not finite-sample calibrated confidence intervals. A Wald interval for a variance near zero or a ZIP probability near zero is especially suspect. Boundary parameters have nonstandard null distributions, so ordinary chi-square or normal reference distributions should not be assumed without justification.

6.2 Post-fit PEV and computational separation

The Laplace fit avoids computing PEV or a full inverse during optimization. This keeps potentially expensive uncertainty calculations out of the likelihood iterations. Once fitting is finished, postPEV() can calculate the joint fixed/random coefficient curvature approximation:

fit_with_pev <- postPEV(fit_laplace, mode = 1L)
head(fit_with_pev$uPevList)

# Request the dense coefficient covariance only when its size is appropriate.
fit_with_full_covariance <- postPEV(fit_laplace, mode = 2L)
dim(fit_with_full_covariance$Ci)

Mode 1 stores random-effect prediction-error variances without retaining a dense full coefficient covariance. Mode 2 also materializes the full joint coefficient covariance and is therefore subject to a dense-memory guard. Mode 0 removes stored PEV/covariance output. These post-fit coefficient curvature calculations do not rerun or alter the fitted parameter estimates. They are distinct from the numerical outer-parameter Hessian used for fixed-effect, covariance-parameter, and family-parameter standard errors.

As with any approximate latent-variable model, PEV is conditional on the fitted model and its local curvature. It should not be presented as including all sources of uncertainty or as a substitute for external validation.

6.3 Prediction targets

For native Laplace fits, the prediction interface distinguishes:

  • Conditional prediction (re.form=NULL): includes fitted conditional modes for known random-effect levels.
  • Zero-random-effect prediction (re.form=NA): sets the random effects to zero. On a nonlinear link, this is generally not a population mean.
  • Restricted population prediction (re.form="population", type="response"): integrates over supported random-intercept distributions for response-scale means.

The population integration is currently restricted to independent random-intercept terms with identity relationship precision. Other covariance structures fail explicitly for this prediction target. Conditional and zero-random-effect se.fit=TRUE predictions use post-fit local uncertainty; cov.fit=TRUE additionally requests a full prediction covariance subject to the dense-memory limit. Response-scale uncertainty uses a delta method. Uncertainty for general population integration is not implemented.

For ZIP fits with a nontrivial fixed-effects zero formula, link- and response-scale uncertainty propagate the full outer-parameter covariance, including zero coefficients and cross-covariances. Conditional predictions additionally propagate the fitted mode’s parameter dependence and its local conditional latent covariance. This is a post-fit local approximation, not an exact posterior or a future-response prediction interval. The legacy scalar-ZIP coefficient-based prediction approximation remains unchanged.

Other native-family prediction approximations condition on fitted family and covariance parameters except where the documented restricted population prediction propagates its available curvature information. New levels cannot be assigned fitted conditional modes; use zero-random-effect or a supported population target when that matches the question.

7. Diagnostics and validation

7.1 Numerical diagnostics

At minimum, inspect:

  1. Whether the optimizer and conditional-mode iteration converged.
  2. The marginal score/gradient and any rejected evaluations.
  3. Boundary flags and covariance estimates relative to their scale.
  4. Whether requested standard errors are available and whether their curvature is plausible.
  5. Sensitivity to reasonable starting values and model simplifications.

The Laplace diagnostics distinguish outer convergence, mode convergence, curvature validity, uncertainty validity, boundaries, and rejected proposals. They answer numerical questions. They do not prove model identifiability, correct likelihood specification, calibrated uncertainty, or adequate population-level prediction.

7.2 Response diagnostics

Randomized quantile residuals transform a discrete response through its fitted conditional CDF, randomizing within the probability mass at the observed value. Under a correctly specified model they should be broadly compatible with a standard normal distribution, subject to dependence and parameter estimation. Simulation can compare observed patterns with replicates from the fitted response model:

rq <- residuals(fit_laplace, type = "quantile")
replicates <- simulate(fit_laplace, nsim = 100)

Conditional simulations hold fitted latent modes fixed. Population simulations draw new random effects from the fitted covariance model before sampling responses. Neither includes parameter-estimation uncertainty. Check residual patterns against fitted values, covariates, clusters, time, exposure, and design strata; a marginal histogram alone can hide a conditional misspecification.

7.3 Statistical calibration, particularly for ZIP

Simulation is especially important when parameters are weakly identified or lie on boundaries. A useful calibration design varies sample size, cluster count, mean response rate, random-effect variance, and the true structural-zero probability. It should record not just optimizer convergence, but also bias, interval coverage when intervals are justified, boundary frequency, uncertainty availability, variance-component recovery, and predictive diagnostics.

For ZIP, include the Poisson boundary \(\pi=0\) and plausible alternatives near it. The null distribution of the zero-inflation estimate is not an ordinary interior normal distribution. Also test scenarios in which the true zero probability varies with covariates while fitting the current intercept-only model. This measures the consequences of misspecification; it does not by itself establish that adding a formula is the right remedy. Compare against scientifically plausible alternatives, including a better count mean, exposure offset, NB2 overdispersion, and omitted cluster or observation structure.

The implemented fixed-effects formula was subsequently evaluated on 1,800 paired datasets, with 300 replicates per scenario and a preregistered contract. Three moderate-rate scenarios passed every gate. A low-rate scenario did not: only 81.3% of datasets supplied joint SEs, even though zero-slope coverage among available intervals was 93.9%. Across all planned replicates, only 76.3% both supplied an interval and covered the true zero slope. This illustrates why selected-subset coverage, convergence and uncertainty availability must be reported separately. It also limits the current formula extension’s calibration envelope; it does not license zero-component random effects or additional mixture families.

Model comparisons require care. Native Laplace uses ML and can provide likelihood-based summaries, but variance-component tests at boundaries have nonstandard reference distributions. For these cases, parametric bootstrap or a dedicated calibration is preferable to an unqualified standard likelihood-ratio test.

8. A practical modeling workflow

  1. Define the estimand. Decide whether the scientific question concerns conditional effects, subject-specific predictions, or a population average.
  2. Choose the response model. Check the outcome support, trial counts, offsets, exposure, mean-variance relation, and whether extra zeros have a defensible structural interpretation.
  3. Specify random effects scientifically. Use the covariance and relationship structures that represent the design and dependence, not simply the largest available structure.
  4. Choose the fitting approximation deliberately. PQL is the default and reuses the established Gaussian solver; native Laplace provides an approximate marginal ML likelihood for its supported set and may be preferable when likelihood-based inference is central.
  5. Check identifiability and stability. Inspect convergence, gradients, boundaries, uncertainty, starts, and model sensitivity. Treat numerical success separately from statistical validation.
  6. Keep uncertainty post-fit when using Laplace. Fit with output$inverse=0, then request summaries, prediction uncertainty, or postPEV() as needed. Respect the memory guard for dense covariance outputs.
  7. Validate predictions. Use response-scale simulations and design-aware residual checks. For population predictions, ensure the integration target and supported covariance assumptions match the question.
  8. Report the approximation. State the family/link, covariance structures, estimation method, optimization controls, boundary behavior, and whether inference is conditional, marginal, approximate, or simulation-calibrated.

9. Reporting template

A transparent GLMM report should state:

  • the conditional response distribution, link, offsets, trial counts, and any estimated family parameters;
  • the fixed-effects formula and the random-effect covariance/relationship structures;
  • whether estimates used PQL or native Laplace ML, including relevant controls and software version;
  • convergence, mode and boundary diagnostics, and how uncertainty was calculated;
  • the prediction target (conditional, zero random effect, or population-integrated) and any integration restrictions;
  • validation, calibration, residual and simulation checks, plus known limitations.

For zero-inflated Poisson models, additionally report the interpretation of the structural-zero state, whether its probability was fixed or estimated, the boundary behavior and uncertainty limitations, and the evidence supporting the mixture rather than a different count or dependence model.

10. Further reading

The following references provide broader treatments of the statistical ideas behind GLMMs, quasi-likelihood, and likelihood approximations:

  • Breslow, N. E. and Clayton, D. G. (1993). Approximate inference in generalized linear mixed models. Journal of the American Statistical Association, 88, 9–25.
  • McCulloch, C. E., Searle, S. R., and Neuhaus, J. M. (2008). Generalized, Linear, and Mixed Models, second edition. Wiley.
  • McCulloch, C. E. and Neuhaus, J. M. (2011). Prediction of random effects in linear and generalized linear models under model misspecification. Biometrics, 67, 270–279.
  • Pinheiro, J. C. and Bates, D. M. (2000). Mixed-Effects Models in S and S-PLUS. Springer.
  • Wolfinger, R. and O’Connell, M. (1993). Generalized linear mixed models: a pseudo-likelihood approach. Journal of Statistical Computation and Simulation, 48, 233–243.

The method-specific restrictions and implementation details in this vignette describe sommer’s current GLMM interfaces; consult the package release documentation when reproducing an analysis.
